turns.t: Good morning, Singapore — it's Monday, the second of November. This is The Meridian Briefing.
Twelve desks. One world. Twenty minutes — let's go.
Three headlines. Iran has cut its timetable for reopening the Strait of Hormuz from seven days to two.
[curious] Two days. That's the first movement on that number since the blockade started.
Meta and Microsoft raised sixty-two and a half billion dollars on the same day, and told the regulator it was for general corporate purposes.
[deadpan] General corporate purposes. Sixty-two and a half billion.
And a watchmaker in Saxony launched a watch and declined to say what it costs. Four magazines printed four different prices.
[laughs] Okay. I already know what the spine is.

The unstated number. It's in eight desks today. Start with Hormuz. Iran's foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, said on Sunday that Tehran's timetable for partially reopening the strait had fallen from seven days to two.
What did he want for it?

Nothing new. Lift the naval blockade, restore the June oil waivers, unfreeze the assets abroad, thin the American military presence, recognise an Iran–Oman arrangement over the strait, and stop the fighting everywhere.
So the demands held and only the clock moved.
The clock moved. Everything around it got worse.
Go on.
Friday the thirtieth, a tanker caught fire about twenty-five nautical miles north-east of Khasab. A small boat came alongside and attached two explosive devices to the hull.
[exhales] Attached. Not fired at. Somebody came alongside.
Qatar's foreign ministry called it a dangerous act that threatens the safety of maritime navigation, and said it reserves its right to take all necessary measures.
The mediator threatening consequences. Nobody led with that.

Nobody led with that. On the thirty-first a gas vessel was hit forty nautical miles south of Lavan Island, and the Revolutionary Guard's navy escalated a claim from two tankers struck by mines to four.
And Britain?
And then on Sunday Tehran designated Britain's Royal Navy, Royal Air Force and Secret Intelligence Service as terrorist and hostile entities.
Because of the bases.
The day after the midterms. And I want to be careful here — that date rests on anonymous officials and a White House that said it does not comment.
[curious] So what's the danger here?
Andreas Krieg at King's College names it: Iran may become willing to compromise exactly when Washington becomes willing to strike. That's the asymmetry.
Alright. Here's the thing I want to push on. The oil price. It must have gone vertical.
Brent closed Friday at a hundred and thirteen dollars and forty-three cents, up two point three seven per cent on the day and thirteen per cent across October.
That's a lot.
Below March. And here is the number that made this desk sit up. Gold fell three point six two per cent in a single day, to a thirteen-month low.
Gold fell. In a Gulf war week.

Gold fell. And the gap between what American government bonds pay and what inflation-protected ones pay — the market's own forecast of inflation over the next decade — narrowed. From two point three eight per cent to two point three four.
Narrowed. So the bond market is saying this is not an inflation shock.
That is exactly what it is saying.
Then what is it?

The oil is moving. What has exploded is the cost of moving it. Hire for a supertanker from the Gulf of Oman to Asia went from about two hundred and forty-nine thousand dollars a day in early September to over nine hundred thousand.
Nine hundred thousand dollars a day.
About twenty dollars of pure nerves. Historically those stretches have lasted about three point eight months.
[wry] So who's wrong?
One of them is wrong. The oil market is pricing a hostage situation. The bond market is pricing a toll booth.
And the resolution is a date.
The third of November, when Americans vote. And the fourth.
Right — the money block. Singapore first.

Wilmar International told the market on Friday that it sold fertiliser and diesel to six of the ten companies the environment agency has served over the Indonesian fires. About twenty-two and a half million US dollars of revenue last financial year.
That's the first actual number on the relationship.
It is. Wilmar says none of the ten is a subsidiary and it has no operational or supply-chain tie to the six buyers.
And where does the audit stand?
Five have agreed to appoint — and to pay for — investigators into their own operations. Two more are willing. Three have not been named as agreeing at all.
[skeptical] They pay for the people who investigate them.
They pay for them. From a roster the agency picks. And the report goes to the agency.
Does the state have any power to make them?

Now the money number of the day, and it is American. The Bureau of Economic Analysis published its September household accounts on Thursday. Americans spent a hundred and thirteen point one billion dollars more that month than in August.
A big month.
Adjusted for price rises, they took home two point six billion dollars more in actual goods and services.
[pause] Two point six. Out of a hundred and thirteen.
Which the bureau's own table rounds to zero.
So they spent it and got nothing.
Forty per cent of the increase was petrol and other energy goods — forty-five point seven billion dollars of it. Cars went the other way, down fourteen billion.
And the Fed?
It held, ten votes to two — and both dissenters wanted a rise. Inflation is three point six per cent over the year, and the economy grew at an annual rate of three point four in the third quarter.
[thoughtful] Growth, with a consumer standing still.
The regime, named plainly: higher-for-longer, with growth.
Technology. Tell me about the sixty-two and a half billion.

Thursday the twenty-ninth. Meta sold shares and a convertible preferred worth about thirty-seven and a half billion dollars. Microsoft priced a twenty-five billion dollar bond, its first in the United States since two thousand and seventeen.
And the stated purpose.
General corporate purposes. In neither prospectus does the phrase data centre appear as a use of proceeds.
[scoffs] Everybody knows what it is for.

Everybody knows. But a prospectus is the document an investor can sue on. Meta's own description of how it funds itself is — a balanced mix of operating cash flow, investment-grade debt, strategic partnerships, and equity capital.
The thing being built isn't in the sentence.

The thing being built is not in the sentence. And there is a second blank. The prospectus Microsoft filed on the twenty-ninth printed every one of its ten amounts as dollar-sign, aggregate principal amount, and every coupon as per cent per annum.
[gasps] Blank? All of them?
All ten. Under a legend reading, subject to completion. The numbers arrived the next day in a pricing supplement.
And this rhymes with something.

The opposite of what you'd expect. The same week, Microsoft cut its full-year capital-spending forecast, to a hundred and seventy billion from a hundred and seventy-five. Alphabet held guidance below estimates.
If demand were the constraint, the guidance would go up.
It went down. This looks like a financing window being used before it shuts, not a demand signal.
[thoughtful] And what did the engineers make of it?
Nothing. A search of Hacker News across the whole window returns zero stories on either deal.
[laughs] Zero.
Mistral gave away the weights of its biggest model on the twenty-ninth and did not say how much memory it needs. No file size, no download size, no requirement.
For a model you're meant to run yourself.
And the page advises that if running it yourself is subpar, you should use the company's paid service instead.
[wry] Helpful.

Then on Sunday a small outfit called Inferencer Labs published the first measured number anyone has: about fourteen and a half tokens a second on an Apple M three Ultra, in a working set of roughly four hundred and twenty-seven gigabytes.
Is that trustworthy? They made the thing they measured.
Neither of them Mistral.
And the catch?
The quality table attached to that speed figure is not for this model. The page says the figures are from the conversion of a different model entirely, citing time constraints.
[sighs] So the speed is for one model and the quality is for another.
On the maker's own page.
Take my hand. We're going down the rabbit hole.
[deadpan] Every morning with this one.
What have we got?
Rug tufting. Making a rug with a machine the size and noise of a cordless drill.
[excited] Oh, I've seen these. The gun, the big stretched cloth, the yarn going through.

You stretch a sheet of woven cloth onto a frame until it is drum-tight — that's the trade's own word, and the tension is the thing beginners get wrong. Then you draw on the back while the gun punches yarn through hundreds of times a minute.
And the pile grows on the front.

The part nobody films. You brush adhesive across the whole back and wait twelve to forty-eight hours for it to cure before it comes off the frame. Then you shear it flat and carve valleys between the colour blocks.
[thoughtful] Is anyone honest about the toll it takes?

It gets more honest. Tim Eads, who co-founded the largest Western supplier, told a Philadelphia outlet that long-term hand tufting really destroys your body. He has carpal tunnel. He bought a computer-controlled machine instead.
[thoughtful] The man who sells the guns stopped using them.

The real floor is a pair of machines at a hundred and sixty-five US dollars each — one cuts, one loops. The one to actually buy is the Duo, and here is the trap: it comes in three prices and those are not three settings.
They're three different machines.

A German firm builds gantries weighing up to two thousand kilograms and publishes no price at all. And a startup claims the first desktop machine at about nine thousand dollars — every variant of which reads sold out, because it is not shipping.
[amused] Not shipping.
The same pneumatic machine sells for eleven hundred and forty-nine dollars at one retailer and twenty-one hundred at another. Read on the same day.
[gasps] Eighty-three per cent apart. For the identical thing.
There is no price discipline in this market at all.
And can you make money?
Barely. The best-priced commission artist charges sixty to a hundred dollars a square foot — and her page currently says, sorry, not taking submissions.
She's shut.
People make money in tufting by teaching it and by selling supplies to the people who just learned. Which is what every surviving business in the piece actually does.
And a Singapore scene?

A real one. About You Studio in Bugis does forty-five minutes for fifty-five dollars and you take the rug home that evening — that's the hook. But of ten studios one guide listed, five are closed or paused.
[pause] Half.
A fifty per cent studio mortality rate in one city is the thing the viral-craft coverage never writes.
Culture, quickly.
A documentary about Elizabeth Holmes reached number one at the American box office for the first time. By two hundred thousand, six hundred and eighty-four dollars.
That's a rounding error.
It is. And these are Sunday estimates with the finals due Monday. It also won the third-lowest weekend of the year, in a year running more than seventeen per cent ahead.
So it's a shrinking denominator.
And one film opened on Halloween to nothing. Zero per cent, from twenty-six critics.
[laughs] Zero per cent.

The family desk, and this one matters. The journal Pediatrics published the largest study yet of heavy social media use in young adolescents. Eleven thousand two hundred and seventy-nine of them, average age twelve point zero one.
Exactly our reader's daughter.
Exactly. Across four annual transitions, heavy use predicted later depression in two of them, at effect sizes of zero point zero six and zero point zero seven.
Small.
Nothing. Not one of the four intervals excluded zero.
[pause] Not one.

There's a second paper, published Friday, that gives something concrete. Five thousand two hundred and ninety-eight children averaging twelve and a half. Two behaviours tracked with less sadness, and it names them: having dinner together, and talking with parents about plans.
[warmly] Dinner and plans.
Dinner and plans. Household conflict went the other way, and so did time texting and on video calls.
Any catch?
Two. The paper publishes directions and probabilities only — no effect sizes at all, so the size is unknown. And the fieldwork was May and August of twenty-twenty.
A lockdown cohort.
Those twelve-year-olds are eighteen now. In twenty-twenty a video call was a substitute for school. In twenty-twenty-six it is an addition to it.
And the disclosure?
Print it. One author on the Pediatrics paper is currently serving as an expert witness in social media litigation.
[thoughtful] That doesn't make them wrong. It makes it worth knowing.
General guidance, not medical advice.
Fitness. One thing.
A meta-analysis says the hours just above a comfortable pace did roughly twice as much as the hours below it. Thirty-eight point seven per cent improvement against eighteen point four.
That's against the whole easy-hour religion.
The studies substantially disagree with each other. The authors say their recommendation seems to be recommended. Those are their words.
[laughs] Seems to be.
Not medical advice. Talk to your own trainer and your own doctor.
[thoughtful] Alright. Take us down.
Taiwan is winning its war on fraud. Reported cases fell thirteen per cent in September; losses fell nearly twenty-nine.
That's a real win.
Since a two thousand and twenty-three amendment, handing over your bank account without good reason is dealt with not by a court but by an administrative admonition, issued by a police agency.
No trial.

No trial, no conviction, no criminal record. What there is, is a schedule. Five years. Ten thousand New Taiwan dollars a day at the cash machine. No internet banking, no telephone banking, no payment apps. No bank may open you a new account. Crypto accounts closed.
[drawn out] For five years.
A hundred and twenty-four thousand, six hundred and seventeen. Three thousand nine hundred and thirty-seven appealed. About one per cent succeeded.
One per cent. [pause] In a country where everything is cashless.

Is a different one, and it is falling. Frozen accounts, from about sixty-four thousand in twenty-twenty-one to a peak near a hundred and fifty-four thousand, down to a hundred and thirty-three thousand by the middle of this year. The regulator made that count a supervisory target for banks.
So the number they measure went down.

The number they measure went down. Nobody keeps a count of wrongly frozen accounts. And the register of admonished people keeps growing, because an admonition lasts five years and does not expire when a freeze lifts.
[thoughtful] Reporting the falling one and compounding the rising one.
And here is the turn. The crackdown made a clean account scarce, so the price of one went from about two thousand New Taiwan dollars in twenty-twenty-four to a ceiling of six hundred thousand.
More than thirtyfold?

More than thirtyfold in two years. And then the market moved on — the investigators now say the rings have largely stopped buying passbooks and phish a password instead. So the five-year penalty is calibrated for a crime nobody commits any more, and its subjects are increasingly people who sold nothing. A man listed spare baseball tickets, gave a buyer his account number, got suspicious and stopped replying. The ring used the account anyway. Up to six hundred thousand frozen the same day, including his student-loan repayments.
[exhales] And the clearest sign of what it's done?
Four thousand seven hundred people have signed a petition asking the state for the right to refuse incoming money.
[pause] Not to send it.
To refuse it. In a high-trust democracy with one of the world's most digitised payment systems, an unsolicited one-dollar deposit has become a thing to be afraid of.
And South Korea already ran this.
Taiwan has built the detection and has not built the clock. Its law says reasonable period. The regulation gives no length at all.
[thoughtful] And the honest line?

Concede the effectiveness. What's left is narrower and sharper. A five-year deprivation of financial function, set by regulation, imposed by police, with a one per cent appeal rate, no deadline anywhere, and no published count of the wrongly caught.
What a state measures, it manages.
What it declines to count is the part you have to go and find.
[pause] That's the issue.
That's the issue. That's the Briefing. The full book is on your dashboard — twenty-four pages, footnotes and all.
Read the footnotes. See you tomorrow, Singapore.
